source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)

topics.title: § 3.3.4 — Separation of Functions, Ex Parte Advice and Record Exclusivity (pp. 123–133)
topics.description: Assigned textbook material: Quintanar opinion, Consumer Advocate excerpt, Withrow note, federal/state APA standards, and Baxter/QZT hypothetical.

entries.title: Separation of functions — three types of agency personnel
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Adversaries (investigators, prosecutors, advocates), adjudicators (ALJs and agency heads), and nonadversarial staff are treated differently in the same pending case.
entries.laymanExplanation: The employee who prosecuted the case cannot secretly advise the judge, but an uninvolved staff expert often can.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal APA § 554(d) and analogous state APAs generally forbid staff adversaries from participating in adjudication or advising decisionmakers off record; nonadversarial advisers may assist, subject to record exclusivity and statutory limits.
entries.examApplication: For every communicator, identify role in this SAME case and whether message reached ALJ, agency head, or advisor.
entries.examTrap: Staff involvement in a similar but different case does not automatically disqualify.

entries.title: A unitary agency can investigate, prosecute and judge if different people perform conflicting roles
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Administrative agencies may combine enforcement and adjudication institutionally; procedural rules require limited internal separation at the individual-case level.
entries.laymanExplanation: The agency does not need to break into separate organizations, but its prosecutor cannot be the secret adviser for a case being decided.
entries.legalExplanation: Quintanar allows a single Department to retain all functions while separating the individuals who acted as adversaries from the final decision-maker's confidential substantive advice.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish institutional combination of powers from personal staff-level conflict.
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse internal separation with a constitutional requirement for two separate agencies.

entries.title: Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control v. ABC Appeals Board (Quintanar), 145 P.3d 462 (Cal. 2006)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: No. California APA's ex parte restrictions apply through final agency decision and forbid substantive off-record contact from case prosecutor to final decisionmaker or adviser; the unauthorized submission itself is improper, without proof director relied on it. Order reversed, Appeals Board affirmed; sweeping mandatory screening remedy was too broad.
entries.laymanExplanation: Case prosecutor may not privately give merits advice to ALJ/agency head or decisionmaker's adviser; the ex parte submission violates applicable California APA even if reliance cannot be shown.
entries.legalExplanation: California's 1995 adjudication statute preserves neutral decisionmaking and exclusive hearing record. Agency heads may consult nonadversarial staff; allow ordinary procedural matters and served posthearing briefs; agency may continue reports if shared with parties and opportunity to respond. Department's refusal to produce reports prevented ordinary proof, but court did not require a showing of influence. Court declined harmless-error treatment.
entries.examApplication: Track roles, timing, substance, service and record. Remedy: reverse improper decision, not necessarily wholesale restructuring.
entries.examTrap: Do not say a unitary agency is unconstitutional, that every off-record staff contact is forbidden, or that challenger must prove actual influence.
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpted in assigned textbook pages
entries.facts: California ABC Department prosecuted Quintanar for allegedly serving visibly intoxicated patrons. After ALJ ruled for licensee, Director reversed and suspended the license. Prosecutor routinely prepared a confidential 'report of hearing' with hearing summary and recommendation for Director. Independent Appeals Board reversed the Director; department refused requests to disclose its reports.
entries.issue: May the prosecutor in an administrative license adjudication send a confidential substantive report to the agency's final decisionmaker after ALJ hearing, without serving licensee or permitting response?
entries.holding: No. California APA's ex parte restrictions apply through final agency decision and forbid substantive off-record contact from case prosecutor to final decisionmaker or adviser; the unauthorized submission itself is improper, without proof director relied on it. Order reversed, Appeals Board affirmed; sweeping mandatory screening remedy was too broad.
entries.reasoning: California's 1995 adjudication statute preserves neutral decisionmaking and exclusive hearing record. Agency heads may consult nonadversarial staff; allow ordinary procedural matters and served posthearing briefs; agency may continue reports if shared with parties and opportunity to respond. Department's refusal to produce reports prevented ordinary proof, but court did not require a showing of influence. Court declined harmless-error treatment.
entries.rule: Case prosecutor may not privately give merits advice to ALJ/agency head or decisionmaker's adviser; the ex parte submission violates applicable California APA even if reliance cannot be shown.

entries.title: Ex parte rule extends to agency head's final decisional stage
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: The ex parte prohibition is not limited to ALJ's trial-stage hearing; it applies to director or delegee considering proposed decision.
entries.laymanExplanation: The prosecutor cannot privately lobby the boss after the judge finishes hearing the case.
entries.legalExplanation: Quintanar reasoned California's article 7 extends decision-maker restrictions to agency heads and their advisers.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether communication occurred while still pending before final decision.
entries.examTrap: Do not end analysis merely because ALJ hearing already concluded.

entries.title: Submission alone unlawful; no proof of actual consideration
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Where California APA forbids substantive prosecutor-to-decisionmaker contact, improper transmission is enough even without demonstrating decisionmaker relied on it.
entries.laymanExplanation: You don't have to prove the secret note changed the result—the improper secret note itself breaks the rule.
entries.legalExplanation: Actual influence is difficult to prove without forbidden inquiry into mental processes. Agency cannot claim that undisclosed message was ignored as a legal shield.
entries.examApplication: Explain prejudice/remedy separately; in Quintanar court refused harmless error.
entries.examTrap: This is a state statutory holding, not proof all federal courts apply automatic reversal in every ex parte case.

entries.title: Permitted communications: procedural, served briefs, or nonadversarial advice
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Uncontroversial scheduling/procedure and on-the-record filings shared with parties are allowed; nonadversarial staff may advise head using record without adding evidence.
entries.laymanExplanation: The judge can ask a neutral specialist for technical help, or read a brief both sides received.
entries.legalExplanation: Substance, role, timing and opportunity for adversarial response determine legality, not mere contact between co-workers.
entries.examApplication: Compare (a) secret prosecutor recommendation, (b) fully served prosecutor brief, (c) neutral scientist explanation.
entries.examTrap: Even neutral adviser cannot secretly inject outside facts into exclusive record.

entries.title: Court review of suspected irregularity may require extra-record evidence
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: To investigate credible procedural irregularity in decision-making, review may go beyond usual administrative record despite ordinary record-based review.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may need to see the secret report to prove illegal private contact.
entries.legalExplanation: Quintanar approved Appeals Board order to produce hearing reports for the specific procedural irregularity allegation.
entries.examApplication: Spot refusal to disclose secret communications.
entries.examTrap: An ordinary merits appeal doesn't automatically permit discovery into all agency deliberations.

entries.title: Consumer Advocate Division v. Tennessee Regulatory Authority, 1998 Tenn. App. LEXIS 428
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: No. TRA may privately receive staff advice interpreting its record; these nonadversarial communications were protected against requested discovery under Tennessee statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: Unlike Quintanar, adviser did not advocate in pending case; check state statutory definition of permitted staff assistance.
entries.legalExplanation: Utility rate issues are technical and agency heads cannot reasonably be expected to independently master long expert record; law permits advice from competent uninvolved staff, analogous to judicial clerks, without furnishing new evidence.
entries.examApplication: A confidential expert recommendation is not forbidden merely because it takes a position on merits; adding outside evidence would be different.
entries.examTrap: Short appellate excerpt, not a complete published opinion in uploaded text
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpted in assigned textbook pages
entries.facts: TRA approved Nashville Gas rate increases. Authority directors consulted their own staff who had not served as prosecutors or investigators, obtaining confidential recommendations on complicated finance, accounting and utility questions. Consumer Advocate Division demanded discovery of communications.
entries.issue: Do confidential recommendations from previously uninvolved agency technical staff to deciding commissioners violate separation of functions or require disclosure?
entries.holding: No. TRA may privately receive staff advice interpreting its record; these nonadversarial communications were protected against requested discovery under Tennessee statute.
entries.reasoning: Utility rate issues are technical and agency heads cannot reasonably be expected to independently master long expert record; law permits advice from competent uninvolved staff, analogous to judicial clerks, without furnishing new evidence.
entries.rule: Unlike Quintanar, adviser did not advocate in pending case; check state statutory definition of permitted staff assistance.

entries.title: Record exclusivity limits even permitted adviser
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: A nonadversarial adviser may analyze hearing evidence but must not furnish new evidence or modify the official record.
entries.laymanExplanation: An adviser can help make sense of exhibits; cannot secretly add new experiments or rumors.
entries.legalExplanation: Tennessee's updated statute permits staff assistants only if they do not furnish, augment, diminish, or modify evidence; California has similar language. Agency must decide on the exclusive record.
entries.examApplication: Identify if adviser opines on weight/credibility versus independently supplies factual material.
entries.examTrap: Tennessee 1998 permits broader substantive evaluation than 2010 MSAPA.

entries.title: Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35 (1975) — federal due process baseline
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: State medical board investigated Dr. Larkin, then considered revoking his license for alleged illegal abortions; combination of investigative and decisionmaking roles at agency-head level did not itself violate due process.
entries.laymanExplanation: The same board can investigate and later decide: that alone does not show unconstitutional bias.
entries.legalExplanation: Due process does not categorically mandate separation of agency heads' functions; federal APA § 554(d) creates additional staff separation yet expressly exempts agency heads from certain restrictions.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish constitutional due process from stricter statutory APA.
entries.examTrap: Withrow does not mean an individual prosecutor may advise agency head privately contrary to statute.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or quoted in Notes and Questions; no full opinion excerpt in this upload

entries.title: Lyness v. State Board of Medicine, 605 A.2d 1204 (Pa. 1992) — stricter state constitution
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Pennsylvania medical board members voted to initiate charges against doctor, then some members joined final discipline vote. Pennsylvania state constitutional due process disallowed that overlap.
entries.laymanExplanation: A state can demand more independent decisionmakers than federal Constitution requires.
entries.legalExplanation: State court barred agency-head prosecutorial roles that Withrow might allow; compare federal Simpson approach.
entries.examApplication: Flag state constitutional floor higher than federal.
entries.examTrap: Do not import Pennsylvania rule to federal agency case.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or quoted in Notes and Questions; no full opinion excerpt in this upload

entries.title: Baker v. Poughkeepsie City School District — deciding own testimony
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Possible due process exception where agency head testifies against party and later decides whether to credit the head's own testimony.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judge should not judge how truthful the judge's own witness testimony was.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook suggests Withrow may not reach exceptional credibility conflict; New York case divided.
entries.examApplication: Identify direct personal testimony/credibility and available substitute.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume all agency-head charging decisions create this conflict.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or quoted in Notes and Questions; no full opinion excerpt in this upload

entries.title: External separation of functions distinguished from internal separation
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: External separation gives a separate agency authority to hear appeal or case; internal separation keeps enforcement and judging within a unitary agency but bars conflicting participation.
entries.laymanExplanation: Different agency judging your case versus different employees in same agency.
entries.legalExplanation: California ABC Appeals Board is a separate appellate body; agency prosecution remained inside Department at trial and director levels.
entries.examApplication: Compare number of review stages and independent adjudicative body.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat an external appellate body as curing an illegal prior secret report automatically.

entries.title: 1961 MSAPA § 13 personal assistants versus updated staff assistants
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: 1961 model broadly permits agency members to consult other members and personal assistants; some states restrict advice from other staff. Modern amended language permits nonadversarial staff advisers under record constraints.
entries.laymanExplanation: Depending on the state statute, a subject-matter expert may not count as the boss's 'personal assistant.'
entries.legalExplanation: Older statutes can be less hospitable to technical staff than Tennessee's amended law; compare Arnold v Lebel and state-specific law.
entries.examApplication: Examine exactly who gave confidential advice under governing version of MSAPA.
entries.examTrap: Don't treat all model acts as having identical wording.

entries.title: 2010 MSAPA § 408(e)(2) significantly narrows nonadversarial merits advice
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Nonadversarial staff advice limited to technical/scientific explanations, agency policy/procedure/precedent, or communications not weighing evidence quality/sufficiency or witness credibility.
entries.laymanExplanation: A neutral specialist may explain chemistry, but may be barred from saying 'I don't believe the company's witnesses.'
entries.legalExplanation: 2010 model restricted permissible advice more than Tennessee and federal approaches; casebook critiques chilling helpful assistance.
entries.examApplication: Contrast explanation of technical terms with credibility assessment.
entries.examTrap: The 2010 MSAPA restriction is a model statute, not automatically federal law.

entries.title: Federal APA § 554(d): adversary staff versus decisionmakers
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Staff engaged in investigation/prosecution/advocacy cannot in same case participate or advise in decision except where statutory exceptions apply.
entries.laymanExplanation: The agency's prosecuting employee can't secretly be the judge's adviser in that same case.
entries.legalExplanation: Case-specific ban for staff (not blanket employment exclusion) while neutral personnel can give legal and policy help within limits.
entries.examApplication: Classify Sam vs Nancy in Baxter hypothetical and explain applicable exception.
entries.examTrap: Federal agency-head exemption allows heads themselves overlapping roles; it is not general permission for prosecutor staff to advise heads.

entries.title: Federal APA § 554(d)(1): special ALJ bar on ex parte factual consultation
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: ALJ cannot consult ANY person or party on a fact in issue except with notice and chance for all parties to participate; legal/policy advice treated differently.
entries.laymanExplanation: The ALJ's factual record must be shared with litigants even if helper never prosecuted.
entries.legalExplanation: Special restriction attaches to hearing ALJ, not equally agency heads; no blanket ban on asking staff legal or policy questions.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether off-record advice concerned facts, legal reasoning, or policy.
entries.examTrap: Don't mistakenly treat ordinary agency-head staff consultations as identical to an ALJ's factual communication limits.

entries.title: Federal APA § 554(d)(2): ALJ supervision must be free of adversary pressure
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: ALJ may not be supervised by persons who perform investigative or prosecutorial agency functions.
entries.laymanExplanation: The prosecutor cannot be the ALJ's boss and threaten the judge's career for deciding against agency.
entries.legalExplanation: Requires independent line of supervision, guarding against command influence.
entries.examApplication: Consider staffing and reporting hierarchy.
entries.examTrap: Institutional employment by agency alone does not violate this bar.

entries.title: Federal APA § 554(d) exceptions: initial license, rate proceedings, agency heads
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Statute excepts initial licensing and public utility/carrier rate-validity proceedings from some separation requirements, and exempts agency itself or heads from personal role combinations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some formal hearings have exceptions, particularly first licenses and utility rates.
entries.legalExplanation: Read §§ 554(d)(A)–(C) separately: heads may initiate charges and later decide, but adversary staff cannot privately advise heads on pending cases under Attorney General Memorandum interpretation.
entries.examApplication: Check whether Baxter application is an INITIAL license and separately whether Sam's prosecutor role is covered by an applicable exception.
entries.examTrap: An agency-head exception is not carte blanche for adversarial staff; exact subsection and state differences matter.

entries.title: Rule of necessity permits otherwise disqualified official when no substitute
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: A conflicted decisionmaker may nevertheless adjudicate where no lawful alternative is available; delegation to qualified substitute defeats necessity.
entries.laymanExplanation: If the law leaves only one person who can decide, government cannot become paralyzed.
entries.legalExplanation: Lucia footnote 5 notes no need for necessity where other ALJs/Commission can rehear, but suggests the principle might operate if commission itself constitutionally invalid.
entries.examApplication: Identify available statutory delegees, substitutes, alternative boards or judges.
entries.examTrap: Necessity is exception of last resort, not convenience.

entries.title: Key framework: dual challenge of prosecutor/neutral advisers
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Analyze (1) due process actual bias, (2) governing state's ex parte / separation statute, (3) exclusive record, (4) ALJ-specific factual advice prohibition, (5) applicable exceptions and remedy.
entries.laymanExplanation: First ask if the secret adviser helped prosecute THAT case. Then ask what statute regulates the boss and ALJ.
entries.legalExplanation: Baxter QZT problem mixes role of scientific staff, evidence evaluation, staff credibility commentary and initial licensing exception; multiple alternatives produce different legal results.
entries.examApplication: In essay write four headings separately rather than decide 'secret talk = always illegal'.
entries.examTrap: Tennessee staff-merits advice doctrine differs from 2010 MSAPA, California's statute and federal APA.

topics.title: § 3.3.5 — Bias: Personal Interest, Prejudgment and Animus (pp. 133–141)
topics.description: Assigned: Cinderella full opinion, financial interest, factual prejudgment, role-based publicity, hostility, 2010 MSAPA appearance standard, Zen Magnets hypothetical.

entries.title: Bias disqualifies administrative adjudicator under due process and APA
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: A decisionmaker may be disqualified for personal financial or other stake, prejudgment of critical adjudicative facts, or prejudicial hostility toward party; federal APA § 556(b) requires impartial manner and timely sufficient bias affidavit.
entries.laymanExplanation: The agency judge must be fair and cannot enter the case already deciding this particular person is guilty.
entries.legalExplanation: Both ALJs and agency heads may be challenged; because bias is context-sensitive, courts rely on cases to define disqualifying appearance/partiality.
entries.examApplication: Identify exact source and type of bias, when objection made, and resulting remedy.
entries.examTrap: Strong agency mission commitment or familiarity with case in official role is usually insufficient.

entries.title: Timely bias objection or waiver
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Party should raise bias challenge promptly once grounds known; waiting until losing can forfeit claim.
entries.laymanExplanation: Speak up when you learn judge is biased—not only after bad decision.
entries.legalExplanation: APA § 556(b) permits good-faith timely affidavit as part of agency record.
entries.examApplication: Note when press statement, conflict or relationship became known.
entries.examTrap: Late strategic allegations may be waived.

entries.title: Cinderella Career & Finishing Schools, Inc. v. FTC, 425 F.2d 583 (D.C. Cir. 1970)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Yes. A disinterested observer could conclude commissioner already decided particular adjudicative facts; FTC order vacated/remanded for decision without Dixon, despite his vote not being necessary to majority.
entries.laymanExplanation: Disqualification when a disinterested observer may conclude adjudicator has in some measure prejudged particular facts and law; the tribunal must also appear fair.
entries.legalExplanation: Agency may issue neutral publicity that complaint filed on 'reason to believe'; an individual commissioner, while appeal pending, cannot publicly announce conclusions making result appear preordained. One biased member may influence colleagues, so mathematical majority without his vote does not cure defect.
entries.examApplication: Compare general anti-fraud policy speech vs particular case facts, timing of appeal, public audience, and influence on collective decision.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume all strong regulatory views are disqualifying or that one biased commissioner's unneeded vote creates harmless error.
entries.sourceRole: Opinion excerpted in assigned textbook pages
entries.facts: FTC ALJ dismissed deceptive advertising case against Cinderella school, FTC commissioners reversed. While appeal pending, Chairman Paul Rand Dixon publicly criticized five-week college offers and airline-hostess charm schools, closely matching allegations against Cinderella. Court recalled his previous disqualifying conduct in Texaco and American Cyanamid.
entries.issue: Does a commissioner's public speech about very allegations in pending adjudication create disqualifying appearance of prejudgment even if his vote is not decisive?
entries.holding: Yes. A disinterested observer could conclude commissioner already decided particular adjudicative facts; FTC order vacated/remanded for decision without Dixon, despite his vote not being necessary to majority.
entries.reasoning: Agency may issue neutral publicity that complaint filed on 'reason to believe'; an individual commissioner, while appeal pending, cannot publicly announce conclusions making result appear preordained. One biased member may influence colleagues, so mathematical majority without his vote does not cure defect.
entries.rule: Disqualification when a disinterested observer may conclude adjudicator has in some measure prejudged particular facts and law; the tribunal must also appear fair.

entries.title: Cinderella appearance of prejudgment test
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Ask whether disinterested observer could conclude that agency official has in some measure adjudged facts and law of the particular pending case before hearing it.
entries.laymanExplanation: Would a neutral outsider think the commissioner had already chosen who was right?
entries.legalExplanation: Application to similar examples in speech while pending case distinguishes pre-decision merits conclusion from general policy.
entries.examApplication: Quote/recognize the 'disinterested observer' test and compare speaker's statement to specific case.
entries.examTrap: The case doesn't forbid agency members from discussing public policy or announcing charges neutrally.

entries.title: Biased member can infect multi-member commission
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Court must remand where biased member participated, even if the member's vote not necessary, because influence over other members cannot be measured.
entries.laymanExplanation: One biased member can sway discussion in ways you cannot count from vote tally.
entries.legalExplanation: Cinderella remanded to FTC excluding Dixon and rejected notion majority survived by counting votes.
entries.examApplication: Look for whether member participated in deliberation, not just votes.
entries.examTrap: This is not a mechanical harmless-error rule for every procedural flaw.

entries.title: Personal financial and institutional interests
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Personal compensation linked to outcomes or board members' direct professional financial incentive to exclude competitors can require recusal.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judge collecting fines for personal pay is not neutral; professional license competitors deciding your practice may also gain personally.
entries.legalExplanation: Tumey found judge paid by fines, Ward involved mayor budget interest, Gibson independent optometrists protecting market; later Friedman required context-specific assessment rather than blanket invalidation.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish industry experience from direct pecuniary incentive.
entries.examTrap: Not every professional licensure board is inherently disqualified.

entries.title: Tumey v. Ohio, 273 U.S. 510 (1927); Ward v. Monroeville, 409 U.S. 57 (1972)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Financial benefit tied to conviction/fines (directly to judge or municipal budget controlled by mayor) violated impartiality.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judge who gains from fines cannot fairly judge.
entries.legalExplanation: Administrative officials must be free of sufficiently direct financial stake.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or quoted in Notes and Questions; no full opinion excerpt in this upload

entries.title: Gibson v. Berryhill, 411 U.S. 564 (1973); Friedman v. Rogers, 440 U.S. 1 (1979)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Optometrist board with self-interested independent practitioners disqualified from judging corporate competitors; later case required case-specific showing rather than blanket ban.
entries.laymanExplanation: Board members who profit by excluding competitor are suspect, but mere occupational background insufficient.
entries.legalExplanation: Use to analyze professional-license board conflicts.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or quoted in Notes and Questions; no full opinion excerpt in this upload

entries.title: Adjudicative facts versus legislative facts and policy
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Prejudging particular party's contested adjudicative facts can disqualify; holding strong views on law, regulatory values, general policy, or legislative facts ordinarily permitted.
entries.laymanExplanation: Commissioner may believe deceptive colleges are bad; may not proclaim Cinderella specifically fraudulent before deciding its case.
entries.legalExplanation: Agency heads chosen because of their regulatory commitments, so courts distinguish bias toward regulatory mission from case-specific factual decision.
entries.examApplication: Compare speech about industrywide concerns with statement matching pending respondent's alleged specific ads.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat general political or scientific policy preference as proof adjudicative bias.

entries.title: Official-role familiarity is usually not prejudgment
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency judge's prior merits ruling, school board negotiations, or in-role factual exposure usually doesn't alone establish disqualification.
entries.laymanExplanation: You don't have to swap judges simply because they know facts from doing their job.
entries.legalExplanation: NLRB v Donnelly Garment and Hortonville distinguish in-role activities from public prejudging outside role.
entries.examApplication: Ask where facts learned and whether public statement expresses decision on contested private case.
entries.examTrap: An ALJ who rules against respondent and later hears remand is not automatically biased.

entries.title: Hortonville Joint School District v. Hortonville Education Association, 426 U.S. 482 (1976)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Board that negotiated with teachers later disciplined strikers; participation in agency's statutorily assigned role not automatically bias.
entries.laymanExplanation: Work-related familiarity or labor policy viewpoint isn't enough to disqualify.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrast Cinderella's extracurricular speech about pending case.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or quoted in Notes and Questions; no full opinion excerpt in this upload

entries.title: Personal animus — extrajudicial source or exceptionally extreme in-hearing hostility
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Usually hostility warrants recusal if from outside proceedings; exceptionally extreme statements during proceedings can also demonstrate inability to judge fairly.
entries.laymanExplanation: A judge's sharp credibility assessment isn't automatically unfair; humiliating attacks irrelevant to issues may be.
entries.legalExplanation: Liteky supplies extrajudicial-source framework plus extreme-in-proceeding exception; Wang reversed asylum denial where IJ berated applicant for parenting irrelevant to asylum claim.
entries.examApplication: Evaluate remarks' relevance, source, intensity and impact on credibility finding.
entries.examTrap: Do not claim all firm or unfavorable hearing comments establish animus.

entries.title: Wang v. Attorney General, 423 F.3d 260 (3d Cir. 2005)
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Immigration judge aggressively disparaged asylum applicant's parenting of disabled daughter and found him not credible, although issue not relevant to asylum eligibility.
entries.laymanExplanation: When judge attacks personal character irrelevant to law, neutrality may be gone.
entries.legalExplanation: Extreme hearing hostility may establish bias despite in-hearing source.
entries.examApplication: Link remarks to findings and remedy.
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or quoted in Notes and Questions; no full opinion excerpt in this upload

entries.title: Appearance-of-bias standard differs across legal systems
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: 2010 MSAPA § 402(c) expressly permits disqualification for factor causing reasonable observer to question impartiality; federal judicial disqualification under § 455(a) similar, but whether broad standard should apply uniformly to agency heads is debated.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency officials wear many policy hats that judges do not, so even neutral regulatory work may LOOK partisan.
entries.legalExplanation: Textbook argues that importing judicial appearance standard into agency administration can undermine required agency policymaking and enforcement; Cinderella does demand an appearance of fairness in a particular prejudgment context.
entries.examApplication: Differentiate binding 2010 model provision in adopting state from policy debate over federal APA standard.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat textbook debate as controlling federal holding.

entries.title: Agency publicity: neutral 'reason to believe' release vs adjudicator's prejudgment speech
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: Agency announcement that charges have issued can be permissible warning; public claim by decisionmaker that allegations are already proven before deciding case is different.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency can tell customers it filed a complaint; commissioner cannot present respondent's guilt as settled.
entries.legalExplanation: First Cinderella publicity appeal distinguished neutral reporting of proceedings from later case-specific Dixon speech. ACUS Recommendation 73–1 called for careful risk-based notice of adverse publicity.
entries.examApplication: Ask was message official notice or individual's predecision merits condemnation?
entries.examTrap: Adverse publicity can hurt reputation without automatically being judicially reviewable or proving bias.

entries.title: Bias challenge attack framework
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 3, pp. 123–141; user-supplied Chapter 3 continuation (Nov. 24, 2026)
entries.summary: (1) Identify adjudicator and source of law; (2) specify pecuniary stake, facts prejudged, or animus; (3) distinguish institutional policy and ordinary official role; (4) identify timing, waiver, influence and remedy.
entries.laymanExplanation: Ask: who decided, what did they say/do, was it particular facts, and how could it affect tribunal?
entries.legalExplanation: Synthesizes Cinderella, Withrow, Tumey/Ward, Gibson/Friedman, Liteky/Wang and 2010 MSAPA.
entries.examApplication: Apply to separate rulemaking public position and later adjudication of past conduct.
entries.examTrap: Citing 'bias' without distinguishing general policy views from case facts is insufficient.
